$$e^{- \frac{5 \cdot \left(x+2\right)^{3}}{3}}z=3 \cdot e^{- \frac{5 \cdot \left(x+2\right)^{3}}{3}}+C.$$

Thus

$$z=C \cdot e^{\frac{5 \cdot \left(x+2\right)^{3}}{3}} + 3.$$

Finally, substitute $z=y^{5}$ and solve for $y$:

$$y=\sqrt[5]{C \cdot e^{\frac{5 \cdot \left(x+2\right)^{3}}{3}} + 3}.$$

$$\begin{aligned}p(x)&=-1\\ q(x)&=2\\ n&=\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}$$

Divide by $y^{\frac{1}{2}}$ and set $z=y^{\frac{1}{2}}$. The chain rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}=\frac{1}{2 \cdot \sqrt{y}}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}.$$

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}+\left(- \frac{1}{2}\right)z=1.$$

$$I(x)=e^{\int - \frac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{d}x}=e^{- \frac{x}{2}}.$$

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(e^{- \frac{x}{2}}\,z\right)=e^{- \frac{x}{2}}.$$

$$e^{- \frac{x}{2}}z=- 2 \cdot e^{- \frac{x}{2}}+C.$$

Thus

$$z=C \cdot e^{\frac{x}{2}} - 2.$$

Finally, substitute $z=y^{\frac{1}{2}}$ and solve for $y$:

$$y=\left(C \cdot e^{\frac{x}{2}} - 2\right)^{2}.$$

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x)=1,\,q(x)=-x,\,n=3.
$$

First, we divide the differential equation by ${y}^{3},$ and we get

$$
{y}^{-3}\frac{dy}{dx}+{y}^{-2}=-x.\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{-2}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-2{y}^{-3}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{-3}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
-\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+z=-x
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. But first, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-2z=2x
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=-2,\,Q(x)=2x\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (-2)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{-2x}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)={e}^{-2x}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{-2x}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-2z) & ={e}^{-2x}\cdot (2x) \\ {e}^{-2x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-2z{e}^{-2x} & =2x{e}^{-2x} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(z{e}^{-2x}) & =2x{e}^{-2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(z{e}^{-2x})\,\text{d}x & =\int 2x{e}^{-2x}\,\text{d}x \\ z{e}^{-2x} & =-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-2x}(2x+1)+{C}_{1} \\ z & =\frac{C{e}^{2x}-2x-1}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=2{C}_{1}.$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{-2}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{-2}=\frac{C{e}^{2x}-2x-1}{2}\,⇒\,y=\pm \sqrt{\frac{2}{C{e}^{2x}-2x-1}}.\end{aligned}

{y}^{-1/2}\frac{dy}{dx}-{y}^{1/2}=1.\,\,(∗)

Then, we make the substitution

$$

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{-1}.

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-{y}^{-2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{-2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.

$$
-\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{x}z=\sqrt{x}

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{x}z=-\sqrt{x}
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=\frac{1}{x},\,Q(x)=-\sqrt{x}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (1/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & =x\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$

Now, we divide the differential equation by ${y}^{3/4},$ and we get

$$
{y}^{-3/4}\frac{dy}{dx}+{x}^{-1}{y}^{1/4}=x.\,\,(∗)
$$

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{1/4}.

$$

$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{4}{x}^{-1}z=\frac{x}{4}

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x),

with

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (1/4x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{(1/4)\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={x}^{1/4}\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem:
Find the general nonzero real solution to the differential equation

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}+3 \cdot y=3 \cdot \left(x-3\right) \cdot y^{3}.
$$

Work on an interval where $\left(x-3\right)>0$. Choose constants and intervals on which the displayed expressions are real and finite.

{{selection}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
This is a Bernoulli equation with

$$\begin{aligned}p(x)&=3\\ q(x)&=3 \cdot \left(x-3\right)\\ n&=3.\end{aligned}$$

Divide by $y^{3}$ and set $z=y^{-2}$. The chain rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}=- \frac{2}{y^{3}}\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}.$$

Hence the linear equation in standard form is

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}z}{\mathrm{d}x}+\left(-6\right)z=- 6 \cdot \left(x-3\right).$$

An integrating factor is

$$I(x)=e^{\int -6\,\mathrm{d}x}=e^{- 6 \cdot \left(x-3\right)}.$$

Multiplying through and using the product rule gives

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(e^{- 6 \cdot \left(x-3\right)}\,z\right)=- 6 \cdot \left(x-3\right) \cdot e^{- 6 \cdot \left(x-3\right)}.$$

Integrating with respect to $x$, we obtain

$$e^{- 6 \cdot \left(x-3\right)}z=\left(\left(x-3\right) + \frac{1}{6}\right) \cdot e^{- 6 \cdot \left(x-3\right)}+C.$$

Thus

$$z=C \cdot e^{6 \cdot \left(x-3\right)} + \left(x-3\right) + \frac{1}{6}.$$

Finally, substitute $z=y^{-2}$ and solve for $y$:

$$y=\pm\sqrt{\frac{6}{6 \cdot C \cdot e^{6 \cdot \left(x-3\right)} + 6 \cdot \left(x-3\right) + 1}}.$$

Here $C$ is an arbitrary real constant; exclude singularities and restrict to the stated real intervals. Both signs are retained wherever the radicand is positive.
